extracted.subtask_description: Practical craft and process advice for writing fiction (short stories and novels), emphasizing habit, honesty, scene/situation-based creation, and descriptive technique. Focuses on daily practice, finding situations rather than over-plotting, and how to describe and render characters convincingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dedicated writing room / closed door
rubrics_metrics.description: Your writing room needs only one thing: a door which you are willing to shut.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A private, shut room signals commitment and helps you focus. It needn't be luxurious (examples: laundry room, basement); the closed door tells the world and yourself you mean business. Anti-patterns: working in shared, constantly interrupted spaces that make a writing resolution hard to take seriously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set a concrete daily writing goal (1000 words recommended)
rubrics_metrics.description: By the time you step into your new writing space and close the door, you should have settled on a daily writing goal. I suggest a thousand words a day ... you can take one day a week off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the goal modest at first to avoid discouragement; treat the goal as sacrosanct (keep the door closed until it's met). Rationale: momentum, urgency, and habit sustain long-term productivity. Anti-patterns: vague intentions, waiting for the muse, skipping days which erodes urgency and immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habituate a writing schedule (creative sleep / ritual)
rubrics_metrics.description: Your schedule—in at about the same time every day, out when your thousand words are on paper or disk—exists in order to habituate yourself, to make yourself ready to dream just as you make yourself ready to sleep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat writing time like a sleep ritual: same block daily trains mind and body to enter a creative state. Examples: fixed blocks like 'nine ’til noon' or 'seven ’til three'. Benefit: makes spontaneity and creative 'waking-sleep' more likely. Anti-patterns: irregular hours, no ritual, expecting inspiration on demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate distractions in the writing room
rubrics_metrics.description: If possible, there should be no telephone in your writing room, certainly no TV or videogames ... draw the curtains or pull down the shades unless it looks out at a blank wall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove everything that can break focus; for beginners this is especially crucial. Music is acceptable if it helps you 'shut the door' (King works to loud rock as a surround). Anti-patterns: phones, TVs, visible busy windows, and other interrupting devices that fragment attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell the truth in your writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Anything at all … as long as you tell the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honesty about your characters' voices, emotions, and actions is foundational; it compensates for many technical weaknesses. Anti-patterns: inventing feelings or behaviors that ring false; 'lying' about what you know and feel, which will collapse the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write what you know — interpreted broadly
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret 'write what you know' as broadly and inclusively as possible ... the heart also knows things, and so does the imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use your concrete knowledge (jobs, settings, skills) to enrich fiction but don't use it to lecture. Blend personal knowledge of life, relationships, work, etc., into unique stories (example: plumber on a starship). Anti-patterns: wardrobe-inventory lecturing or using knowledge as a substitute for story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write what you love; avoid writing to chase the market
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be very wrong ... to turn away from what you know and like in favor of things you believe will impress ... or to write toward money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow genuine interests and passion rather than market calculations; deliberate chasing of genre for profit tends to produce hollow imitations and moral/intellectual dishonesty. Anti-patterns: plotting choices made primarily for perceived commercial return.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use imitation as a learning tool, not as an aesthetic target
rubrics_metrics.description: Stylistic imitation is one thing, a perfectly honorable way to get started as a writer ... but one cannot imitate a writer's approach to a particular genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitate to learn technique and voice early on, but avoid trying to replicate another author's feeling or market formula; 'in the tradition of' labeling often signals overcalculated imitation. Anti-patterns: producing pale copies of bestsellers by mimicking surface vocabulary or plot mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer situation over plot — excavating found stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories are found things, like fossils in the ground ... The job of the writer is to use the tools in his or her toolbox to get as much of each one out of the ground intact as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with a vivid situation (a 'fossil') and watch characters respond rather than forcing events with a plotted jackhammer. Situational fiction often yields organic incidents and surprises; plotting is a writer's last resort and may produce artificial results. Examples: Misery ('two characters in a house'), Gerald's Game ('one woman in a bedroom'). Anti-patterns: heavy plotting that breaks spontaneity and feels labored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find material with What-If questions
rubrics_metrics.description: The most interesting situations can usually be expressed as a What-if question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concise hypothetical prompts ('What if vampires invaded a small New England village?') to locate situations that can be excavated into stories. This is a practical way to seed situational fiction. Anti-patterns: over-engineered premises that prioritize gimmick over believable stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the three parts of fiction: narration, description, dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories and novels consist of three parts: narration, which moves the story from point A to point B ... description, which creates a sensory reality ... and dialogue, which brings characters to life through their speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance and skillfully deploy all three: narration for movement, description for sensory immersion, dialogue for character and voice. Neglecting any one element weakens the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description: visualize, translate, and strike the right balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Description begins with visualization of what it is you want the reader to experience. It ends with your translating what you see in your mind into words on the page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid thin description (leaves reader bewildered) and overdescription (buries reader in detail). Prefer locale/texture over exhaustive physical inventories; don't substitute wardrobe listings for character. Use a few well-chosen sensory details to stand for everything else. Anti-patterns: pimple-by-pimple or skirt-by-skirt enumerations, gratuitous film-like reveals (e.g., zipper on monster's back).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust your first visualized details; rewrite to refine
rubrics_metrics.description: In most cases, these details will be the first ones that come to mind. Certainly they will do for a start ... If you decide later you’d like to change, add, or delete, you can do so—it’s what rewrite was invented for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely initially on the strongest instant images; they are often the most truthful. Use revision to expand, pare back, or sharpen as necessary. Anti-patterns: overthinking initial images until they lose life; refusing to revise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice unplotted narration to develop intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: Write five or six pages of unplotted narration concerning [a found situation] ... let the situation carry you along.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises that force you to write without an outline build the habit of excavation and improve honesty in speech/behavior. King suggests altering an element (e.g., invert sexes of antagonist/protagonist) and narrating honestly. Anti-patterns: resisting exercises and clinging to outlines when learning spontaneous scene development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty in character voice and behavior is non-negotiable
rubrics_metrics.description: Honesty in storytelling makes up for a great many stylistic faults ... but lying is the great unrepairable fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be truthful about how characters speak and behave; authentic voice creates reader recognition. Lying about motivations or emotions undermines the story at a compositional level. Anti-patterns: contrived dialogue or actions that serve plot rather than character truth.
